Python Project - Prosper Loan Data Exploration¶

by Daniel Ake¶

Introduction¶

This project explores the Prosper Loan dataset using Python to understand borrower characteristics, loan performance, and the factors associated with different lending outcomes.

The project follows a complete data analysis process including data gathering, assessment, cleaning, exploratory data analysis, visualization, and communication of findings.

Project Objectives¶

  • Assess and clean the Prosper Loan dataset for analysis.
  • Explore the distribution of important loan and borrower characteristics.
  • Investigate relationships between key variables.
  • Create meaningful visualizations to communicate patterns and trends.
  • Summarize key findings and insights from the analysis.

The Prosper Loan dataset contains 113,937 loan records and 81 variables.

The dataset includes a combination of numerical, categorical, and Boolean variables. The 81 variables consist of 49 float columns, 12 integer columns, 17 object (categorical/text) columns, and 3 Boolean columns.

The variables describe different aspects of the loans and borrowers, including loan amounts, loan status, borrower characteristics, credit information, loan repayment information, and other lending-related attributes.

Initial assessment also shows that some variables contain missing values, which will be investigated further during the data wrangling and exploration process.

The main feature of interest in this analysis is LoanOriginalAmount, which represents the original amount borrowed.

The analysis will investigate how loan amounts are distributed and how they relate to borrower characteristics such as income, employment status, credit risk and interest rates. This will help identify factors that may be associated with the amount of money borrowers receive.

What features in the dataset do you think will help support your investigation into your feature(s) of interest?¶

Several features will support the investigation of LoanOriginalAmount.

  • StatedMonthlyIncome – to investigate whether borrowers with higher income receive larger loans.
  • EmploymentStatus – to examine whether loan amounts differ across employment categories.
  • ProsperRating (Alpha) and ProsperScore – to investigate how borrower risk ratings relate to loan amounts.
  • BorrowerAPR – to examine the relationship between loan amount and borrowing cost.
  • DebtToIncomeRatio – to determine whether borrowers' existing debt relative to income is associated with loan size.
  • LoanStatus – to compare loan amounts across different repayment outcomes.
  • Term – to examine whether loan duration is associated with the amount borrowed.

These features provide information about borrowers' financial position, credit risk, loan characteristics, and repayment outcomes, which can help explain patterns in the original loan amount.

What is the distribution of the original loan amount?¶

This visualization examines how 'LoanOriginalAmount' is distributed across the Prosper Loan dataset.

In [25]:
plt.figure(figsize=(10,7))
plt.hist(df[ "LoanOriginalAmount"], bins=30, color="orange",edgecolor="black")
plt.title("Distribution of Original Loan Amount")
plt.xlabel("Orignal Loan Amount ($)")
plt.ylabel("Frequency")
plt.show()

Observation¶

The distribution of 'LoanOriginalAmount' is right-skewed(lowest to highest from left to right). Most loans are concentrated at the lower loan amounts, while the number of loans generally decreases as the loan amount increases.

There are noticeable peaks at certain loan amounts, suggesting that some loan sizes were more commonly issued than others. Relatively few loans occur at the higher end of the distribution, with loan amounts extending to approximately $35,000.

This distribution provides a useful foundation for investigating whether borrower characteristics, particularly monthly income, are associated with the amount borrowed.

Discuss the distribution(s) of your variable(s) of interest. Were there any unusual points? Did you need to perform any transformations?¶

This visualization examines the distribution of loans across the different loan term categories in the Prosper Loan dataset. The two main variables of interest are 'StatedMonthlyIncome' and 'LoanOriginalAmount'.

'LoanOriginalAmount' is right-skewed, with most loans concentrated at lower to moderate amounts and fewer loans occurring at higher amounts. The distribution also shows noticeable peaks at certain loan amounts, suggesting that some loan sizes were more common than others.

'StatedMonthlyIncome' is strongly right-skewed. Most borrowers have monthly incomes concentrated around 2,000 to 7,000 dollars, while a small number of borrowers reported extremely high incomes. The initial assessment showed a maximum monthly income of approximately $1.75 million, indicating the presence of substantial outliers.

To make the income distribution easier to interpret, the visualization was restricted to monthly incomes of $30,000 or less. The original data was not deleted or permanently altered; the restriction was applied only to the visualization so that the distribution of the majority of borrowers could be examined more clearly.

Univariate Exploration Summary¶

The univariate analysis examined the distributions of loan amounts, borrower income, loan repayment terms, Prosper credit ratings, and Borrower APR.

The findings showed that 36-month loans were the most common repayment option, followed by 60-month and 12-month loans.

Borrowers’ stated monthly income exhibited a strongly right-skewed distribution, with a small number of exceptionally high-income observations.

To improve the readability of the income visualization, the analysis focused on monthly incomes of $30,000 or less. This filtering was applied only to the visualization, preserving the original dataset.

Missing values were also identified in Borrower APR and Prosper credit ratings. These were excluded from relevant analyses where necessary without modifying the original dataset.

Overall, these adjustments improved the clarity and interpretability of the visualizations.

The most unusual distribution was observed in 'StatedMonthlyIncome', which contained a small number of extremely high income values. These values caused the distribution to be strongly right-skewed and made the main pattern difficult to interpret.¶

To improve the visualization, a filtered version of the data containing monthly incomes of $30,000 or less was used for the histogram. This adjustment was made only for visualization and did not modify or remove observations from the original dataset.

Missing values in variables such as 'BorrowerAPR' and 'ProsperRating (Alpha)' were also identified during the exploration. Missing values were excluded from visualizations where necessary, while the original dataset remained unchanged.

Question: Does income influence loan amount?¶

This visualization investigates the relationship between borrowers' stated monthly income and the original loan amount.

In [35]:
income_loan = df[df['StatedMonthlyIncome'] <= 30000] 
plt.figure(figsize=(10,6))
plt.scatter(income_loan['StatedMonthlyIncome'],
            income_loan['LoanOriginalAmount'],
            alpha=0.3, color= 'purple')
plt.title('Stated Monthly Income Vrs Original Loan Amount')
plt.xlabel('Stated Monthly Income ($)')
plt.ylabel('Original Loan Amount ($)')
plt.show()

Observation¶

The scatter plot suggests a positive relationship between stated monthly income and original loan amount, although the relationship is not strongly linear. Higher-income borrowers appear to have access to larger loan amounts, but borrowers with similar monthly incomes received a wide range of loan amounts.

The horizontal concentrations of points indicate that certain loan amounts were more commonly issued than others. Overall, income appears to be associated with loan amount, but income alone does not fully explain the amount borrowed.

In [36]:
income_loan[['StatedMonthlyIncome','LoanOriginalAmount']].corr()
Out[36]:
StatedMonthlyIncome LoanOriginalAmount
StatedMonthlyIncome 1.000000 0.403898
LoanOriginalAmount 0.403898 1.000000

Correlation Analysis: Monthly Income and Loan Amount¶

The Pearson correlation coefficient between 'StatedMonthlyIncome' and 'LoanOriginalAmount' is approximately 0.404.

This indicates a moderate positive linear relationship between borrowers' stated monthly income and original loan amount.

Although higher-income borrowers generally tend to receive larger loans, the moderate correlation suggests that other factors may also be associated with loan amounts.

The correlation was calculated using records with stated monthly income of $30,000 or less to reduce the influence of extreme income outliers.

Correlation does not establish causation.

In [37]:
rating_order = ['HR', 'E', 'D', 'C', 'B', 'A', 'AA']
plt.figure(figsize=(10,6))
sns.boxplot(data=df,
            x='ProsperRating (Alpha)',
            y='LoanOriginalAmount',
            order=rating_order,
            color='steelblue')
plt.title('Original Loan Amount by Prosper Credit Rating')
plt.xlabel('Prosper Credit Rating')
plt.ylabel('Original Loan Amount ($)')
plt.show()

Observation¶

The box plot reveals a positive association between Prosper credit ratings and original loan amounts. Borrowers with higher credit ratings generally have higher median loan amounts compared with borrowers in lower credit rating categories.

Borrowers rated HR and E have the lowest median loan amounts, while AA-rated borrowers have the highest median loan amount.

The distribution of loan amounts also becomes wider across several higher credit rating categories, indicating greater variability in the amounts borrowed.

Several outliers are visible, particularly among borrowers with higher credit ratings, showing that some loans are substantially larger than the typical amounts within their respective categories.

Overall, the findings suggest that credit rating is associated with loan size. However, other borrower and lending characteristics may also influence the original loan amount.

How does Borrower APR vary across Prosper credit ratings?¶

This visualization investigates the relationship between borrowers’ Prosper credit ratings and their Annual Percentage Rates (APR) to determine whether borrowing costs differ across credit rating categories.

In [39]:
apr_rating = df[['BorrowerAPR','ProsperRating (Alpha)']].dropna()
apr_rating.shape
Out[39]:
(84853, 2)
In [40]:
rating_order = ['HR', 'E', 'D', 'C', 'B', 'A', 'AA']
plt.figure(figsize=(10,6))
sns.boxplot(data=apr_rating, x='ProsperRating (Alpha)', y='BorrowerAPR',order=rating_order, color='chocolate')
plt.title('Borrower APR by Prosper Credit Rating')
plt.xlabel('Prosper Credit Rating')
plt.ylabel('Borrower APR')
plt.show()

Observation¶

The box plot reveals a strong inverse relationship between Prosper credit ratings and Borrower APR. As credit ratings improve from HR to AA, the median Annual Percentage Rate generally decreases.

Borrowers in the HR category have the highest median APR, approximately 35%, while AA-rated borrowers have the lowest median APR, approximately 4%.

The distribution also shows variations in APR within individual credit rating categories, with several outliers indicating that some borrowers receive rates substantially different from the typical rates in their respective categories.

Overall, the findings suggest that borrowers with stronger credit ratings generally benefit from lower borrowing costs, while borrowers with weaker credit ratings tend to face higher APRs.

Business Insight: Credit ratings are strongly associated with loan pricing and may help lending institutions assess borrower risk and understand differences in borrowing costs.

Observation¶

The analysis indicates a positive association between loan repayment duration and original loan amount.

Borrowers with 12-month repayment terms have the lowest median loan amount of 3,500 dollars, followed by 36-month loans with a median of 5,000 dollars. Loans with 60-month repayment terms have the highest median amount of $11,500.

The average loan amounts also increase across the three repayment categories, suggesting that larger loans are more frequently associated with longer repayment periods.

Overall, the findings indicate that loan repayment duration is associated with the amount borrowed, although this relationship does not establish causation.

Business Insight: Understanding the relationship between loan size and repayment duration can help lending institutions evaluate loan structures, repayment arrangements, and lending patterns.

Business Insight: Understanding how APR differs across repayment terms can help lending institutions evaluate loan pricing structures and identify variations in borrowing costs across loan products.

Bivariate Exploration Summary¶

The bivariate analysis investigated relationships between borrower characteristics, credit ratings, loan amounts, repayment terms, and borrowing costs.

  1. Monthly Income and Loan Amount: A moderate positive relationship was observed between stated monthly income and original loan amount, with a Pearson correlation coefficient of approximately 0.404 for borrowers with monthly incomes of $30,000 or less. Higher-income borrowers generally received larger loans, although considerable variation remained.

  2. Credit Rating and Loan Amount: Borrowers with higher Prosper credit ratings generally had higher median loan amounts. AA-rated borrowers had the highest median loan amounts, while HR- and E-rated borrowers had the lowest.

  3. Credit Rating and Borrower APR: A clear inverse relationship was observed. Borrowers with higher credit ratings generally had lower APRs, while borrowers with lower ratings faced higher borrowing costs.

  4. Loan Term and Original Loan Amount: Longer repayment terms were associated with larger loan amounts. The 60-month category had the highest average loan amount, followed by 36-month and 12-month loans.

  5. Loan Term and Borrower APR: APR distributions varied across repayment terms, although the average APRs were relatively similar. The 12-month category had the highest median APR, while the 60-month category had the lowest.

Overall, these findings indicate that credit ratings, borrower income, and repayment terms are associated with differences in loan amounts and borrowing costs. However, these relationships do not establish causation.

Additional Relationships Observed¶

Beyond the primary relationship between stated monthly income and original loan amount, the analysis revealed several interesting associations.

  1. Prosper Credit Rating and Borrower APR: A clear inverse relationship was observed. Borrowers with higher credit ratings generally received lower APRs, while borrowers with lower ratings faced higher borrowing costs. This suggests that credit ratings are an important factor associated with loan pricing.

  2. Loan Repayment Term and Loan Amount: Longer repayment terms were associated with larger original loan amounts. Loans with 60-month repayment periods had higher average loan amounts than loans with 12-month or 36-month terms.

  3. Loan Repayment Term and Borrower APR: Although average APRs were relatively similar across repayment terms, differences were observed in their distributions and median values. This indicates that repayment duration may be associated with variations in borrowing costs.

Overall Finding: These relationships demonstrate that loan characteristics and borrower credit ratings are associated with differences in loan size and borrowing costs. However, further analysis would be required to determine the independent influence of each variable.

Conclusions¶

This project explored the Prosper Loan dataset, containing 113,937 loan records and 81 variables, to investigate the relationship between borrowers’ financial characteristics and original loan amounts.

The analysis used Python, Pandas, Matplotlib, and Seaborn to perform preliminary data assessment, univariate exploration, and bivariate analysis through 10 visualizations.

Key Findings¶

  1. Income and Loan Amount: A moderate positive correlation (r ≈ 0.404) was observed between stated monthly income and original loan amount for borrowers reporting monthly incomes of $30,000 or less. This suggests that higher-income borrowers generally tend to have larger loan amounts, although the relationship is not particularly strong.
  2. Loan Amount Distribution: Original loan amounts were right-skewed, with smaller and moderate-sized loans occurring more frequently than larger loans.
  3. Income Distribution: Stated monthly income was strongly right-skewed, with extreme high-income observations. Filtering income values for visualization improved the readability of the distribution without changing the original dataset.
  4. Credit Ratings: Higher Prosper credit ratings were generally associated with larger median loan amounts and lower borrowing costs.
  5. Loan Repayment Terms: The 36-month repayment term was the most common. Loans with longer repayment periods generally had higher original loan amounts.
  6. Borrowing Costs: Borrower APR varied substantially across credit rating categories, while average APRs were relatively similar across repayment terms.

Answer to the Main Investigation Question¶

The analysis suggests that borrower income is positively associated with original loan amount, but income alone does not fully explain loan size. Credit ratings and loan characteristics also show meaningful associations with loan amounts.

These findings are observational and do not establish that income or any other investigated variable directly causes changes in loan amounts.

Limitations and Further Investigation

The dataset contained missing values and extreme income observations. Some analyses used filtered subsets to improve visualization clarity, so their results may not represent every loan in the original dataset.

Further analysis could investigate additional borrower characteristics and use statistical modeling to better understand the factors independently associated with loan amounts.

Final Reflection¶

This project strengthened practical skills in data assessment, handling missing values, identifying outliers, selecting appropriate visualizations, interpreting statistical relationships, and communicating findings through a structured exploratory data analysis workflow.
